The Guardian goes on the ground with Brazilian forces fighting to eradicate mining that has destroyed protected areas of Indigenous land The jerry-built bordello at the foot of Vila Cururu, an illegal gold-mining settlement at the heart of Brazil’s most desecrated Indigenous territory, was a hive of depravity until just a few weeks ago. Inebriated prospectors huddled around wooden tables, swigging beer and Scotch whisky, and ogling pole-dancing sex workers before going with them to shacks behind the brothel. The encircling encampment also teemed with intruders as hordes of miners used pickaxes and explosives to burrow deep into the hillsides and savanna in search of treasure. “They wiped out everything. They destroyed nature,” said Jackson Katitãurlu, an Indigenous leader from the Nambiquara people, whose village is a few miles from the chaos in the south-western Amazon.

One recent morning, however, Vila Cururu was deserted: the once-bustling illicit community having been razed by Brazilian security forces as they fought to fulfil a pledge by the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to eradicate illegal mining in Indigenous territories after years of mayhem under his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro. As Lula’s eviction tsar, Nilton Tubino, hiked through the encampment’s charred ruins, he recalled how miners fled into the surrounding forests after troops launched a land and air assault in late March to halt one of the most ferocious attacks on Indigenous lands in Brazil’s recent history.

The project was led by two researchers—anthropologist, professor, and Indigenous expert Hanna Limulja and Indigenous researcher Alfredo Himotono Yanomama—and carried out in the Maloca Paapiu region of the Yanomami Indigenous Territory in northern Brazil. Supported by the Impact Seed Fund (ISF), the initiative encouraged reflection on the impacts of illegal mining on Indigenous communities and the Amazon rainforest. During project development, the news report “On Yanomami Land, Young Indigenous People Are Leaving Their Villages To Work in Illegal Mining,” by grantees Victor Raison and Jean-Mathieu Albertini, published by Mongabay, served as a key reference. Supported by the Pulitzer Center, the story documented how miners were attracting young people in 2022 with promises of wealth, drawing them away from their roles as forest guardians—a pattern similar to the experiences described by participants in the podcast.

                      July 7, 2026

Supported by the Pulitzer Center’s Impact Seed Fund (ISF), this project was developed with Indigenous youth in their language, sparking reflection on illegal gold mining in Amazon rainforest communities.

A rare inside look at illegal gold mining reveals how daily work unfolds, how mining camps are organized, and how initial expectations quickly give way to the reality of poor infrastructure and scarce resources for Indigenous people. Yanomami youth who once worked at these sites tell their stories in podcast format, in their language, to speak directly to their own communities.

The project was led by two researchers—anthropologist, professor, and Indigenous expert Hanna Limulja and Indigenous researcher Alfredo Himotono Yanomama—and carried out in the Maloca Paapiu region of the Yanomami Indigenous Territory in northern Brazil. Supported by the Pulitzer Center, the story documented how miners were attracting young people in 2022 with promises of wealth, drawing them away from their roles as forest guardians—a pattern similar to the experiences described by participants in the podcast.

payload.title: Brasilian joukot tuhosivat laittoman kullankaivajaleirin Amazonissa
payload.summary: Vila Cururun laiton kullankaivajayhdyskunta on hävitetty Brasilian turvallisuusjoukkojen operaatiossa. Kaivostoiminta oli vaurioittanut alkuperäiskansojen maita, ja kaivajat pakenivat ympäröiviin metsiin.
payload.content:
Brasilian turvallisuusjoukot ovat tuhonneet Vila Cururun laittoman kullankaivajayhdyskunnan maan lounaisessa Amazonissa. Maaliskuun lopulla alkanut maa- ja ilmaoperaatio ajoi kaivajia ympäröiviin metsiin. Toimilla pyritään toteuttamaan presidentti Luiz Inácio Lula da Silvan lupaus kitkeä laiton kaivostoiminta alkuperäiskansojen alueilta, joilla ympäristö on kärsinyt vakavia vahinkoja.

## Vila Cururu jäi hiiltyneiksi raunioiksi

Ennen operaatiota Vila Cururu oli vilkas, luvattomasti rakennettu asutus. Kaivajat tunkeutuivat hakkujen ja räjähteiden avulla kukkuloihin ja savannille kullan toivossa. Leiriin oli syntynyt myös kaivostoimintaa palvellut bordelli, jossa tarjottiin alkoholia ja seksipalveluja.

Vielä muutamaa viikkoa ennen operaatiota kaivajia kokoontui bordellin puisille pöydille juomaan olutta ja viskiä. Seksityöntekijät veivät asiakkaita rakennuksen takana oleviin majoihin.

Lähellä sijaitsevassa kylässä asuva Nambiquara-kansan johtaja Jackson Katitãurlu kuvasi jälkiä jyrkästi: ”He hävittivät kaiken. He tuhosivat luonnon.”

Kun hallituksen häätöoperaatiota johtava Nilton Tubino kulki myöhemmin alueella, entisestä yhdyskunnasta oli jäljellä hiiltyneitä raunioita. Kaivajat olivat paenneet sotilaiden edeltä ympäröiviin metsiin sen jälkeen, kun joukot aloittivat maa- ja ilmaoperaation maaliskuun lopulla. Paikalla myöhemmin vallinnut hiljaisuus poikkesi jyrkästi leirin aiemmasta vilinästä.

## Nuoria houkuteltiin lupauksilla vauraudesta

Operaatiolla pyritään pysäyttämään yksi Brasilian lähihistorian rajummista hyökkäyksistä alkuperäiskansojen maita vastaan. Presidentti Lula on luvannut poistaa laittoman kaivostoiminnan näiltä alueilta. Toimia on perusteltu vuosien sekasorrolla Jair Bolsonaron presidenttikaudella.

Laittoman kullankaivuun vaikutuksia on tarkasteltu myös Pohjois-Brasilian Yanomami-alueella, joka on eri alue kuin Vila Cururu. Maloca Paapiun seudulla toteutettua hanketta johtivat antropologi ja professori Hanna Limulja sekä alkuperäiskansaan kuuluva tutkija Alfredo Himotono Yanomama. Impact Seed Fundin tukemassa työssä käsiteltiin kaivostoiminnan seurauksia alkuperäisyhteisöille ja Amazonin sademetsälle.

Hankkeen keskeisenä taustana käytetty Victor Raisonin ja Jean-Mathieu Albertinin vuonna 2022 julkaistu reportaasi kuvasi, kuinka kaivajat houkuttelivat alkuperäiskansojen nuoria lupauksilla vauraudesta. Nuoria lähti kylistään kaivoksille ja pois tehtävistään metsän suojelijoina. Podcastiin osallistuneiden kokemuksissa havaittiin samankaltainen kehitys.
summary_bullets: Brasilian joukot tuhosivat Vila Cururun laittoman kullankaivajayhdyskunnan.
Kaivajat pakenivat metsiin maaliskuun lopulla alkaneen maa- ja ilmaoperaation aikana.
Laiton kaivostoiminta vahingoittaa luonnon lisäksi alkuperäisyhteisöjä ja houkuttelee nuoria pois kylistään.

Nuoria lähti kylistään kaivoksille ja pois tehtävistään metsän suojelijoina. Podcastiin osallistuneiden kokemuksissa havaittiin samankaltainen kehitys.

The Guardian goes on the ground with Brazilian forces fighting to eradicate mining that has destroyed protected areas of Indigenous land The jerry-built bordello at the foot of Vila Cururu, an illegal gold-mining settlement at the heart of Brazil’s most desecrated Indigenous territory, was a hive of depravity until just a few weeks ago. Inebriated prospectors huddled around wooden tables, swigging beer and Scotch whisky, and ogling pole-dancing sex workers before going with them to shacks behind the brothel. The encircling encampment also teemed with intruders as hordes of miners used pickaxes and explosives to burrow deep into the hillsides and savanna in search of treasure. “They wiped out everything. They destroyed nature,” said Jackson Katitãurlu, an Indigenous leader from the Nambiquara people, whose village is a few miles from the chaos in the south-western Amazon.

One recent morning, however, Vila Cururu was deserted: the once-bustling illicit community having been razed by Brazilian security forces as they fought to fulfil a pledge by the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to eradicate illegal mining in Indigenous territories after years of mayhem under his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro. As Lula’s eviction tsar, Nilton Tubino, hiked through the encampment’s charred ruins, he recalled how miners fled into the surrounding forests after troops launched a land and air assault in late March to halt one of the most ferocious attacks on Indigenous lands in Brazil’s recent history.

The project was led by two researchers—anthropologist, professor, and Indigenous expert Hanna Limulja and Indigenous researcher Alfredo Himotono Yanomama—and carried out in the Maloca Paapiu region of the Yanomami Indigenous Territory in northern Brazil. Supported by the Impact Seed Fund (ISF), the initiative encouraged reflection on the impacts of illegal mining on Indigenous communities and the Amazon rainforest. During project development, the news report “On Yanomami Land, Young Indigenous People Are Leaving Their Villages To Work in Illegal Mining,” by grantees Victor Raison and Jean-Mathieu Albertini, published by Mongabay, served as a key reference. Supported by the Pulitzer Center, the story documented how miners were attracting young people in 2022 with promises of wealth, drawing them away from their roles as forest guardians—a pattern similar to the experiences described by participants in the podcast.
